Chanos chanos.description: This fish has a long, slightly flattened body with an oval cross‑section. It possesses two dorsal spines followed by 13 to 17 soft dorsal rays, and its anal fin has two spines and eight to ten soft rays. In total, the spine count includes 46 vertebrae. The small, toothless mouth sits low on the head, and a single dorsal fin runs along the middle of the back. Its pectoral fins are shaped like curved blades, while the caudal fin is large and deeply forked. The belly is smooth, lacking any scutes, and there are four branchiostegal rays. The fish’s coloration is olive‑green on the back, silvery along the sides, and the unpaired fins are edged with dark margins.

Thunnus albacares.description: This large, elongated fish has a streamlined, slightly laterally compressed body and a total of 39 vertebrae. It possesses 11 to 14 dorsal spines and 12 to 16 soft rays on the first dorsal fin, while the anal fin has no spines and carries 11 to 16 soft rays. The second dorsal fin is set very close to the first, separated only by a narrow space, and is followed by eight to ten small finlets; the anal fin is likewise followed by seven to ten finlets. In bigger individuals the second dorsal and anal fins can become unusually long, extending to more than 20 % of the fish’s fork length. The pectoral fins are moderately long, typically reaching just beyond the origin of the second dorsal fin and measuring about a quarter of the fish’s length. Between the pelvic fins are two paired flaps known as interpelvic processes. The skin is covered with very small scales, while a subtle band of larger scales forms a faint corselet along the sides. The caudal peduncle is extremely slender and bears a strong lateral keel on each side, flanked by two smaller keels, and the ventral surface of the liver is smooth, lacking any striations. A swim‑bladder is present. In life, the back shines metallic dark blue that fades to yellow toward the sides and becomes silvery on the belly, which often displays about twenty broken, nearly vertical lines. The dorsal and anal fins, together with their finlets, are bright yellow, and each finlet is edged with a thin black border. The overall body shape is fusiform with an oval cross‑section.

Sardinella lemuru.description: This fish has no dorsal or anal spines, with thirteen to twenty‑one soft rays on the dorsal fin and twelve to twenty‑three soft rays on the anal fin. A faint golden spot sits just behind the gill opening, followed by a subtle golden line running along the side of the body, and a clearly defined black spot marks the rear edge of the gill cover where pigment is absent. Its body is elongated and almost cylindrical, giving it a streamlined, fusiform shape, while the cross‑section is laterally compressed. It can be told apart from other clupeid species in the eastern Indian Ocean and western Pacific by having eight pelvic fin rays, and it differs from *Sardinella longiceps* by possessing a shorter head and fewer lower gill rakers.

Oreochromis niloticus.description: This tilapia is a relatively large, deep‑bodied fish with a streamlined, laterally‑compressed shape. It typically has 15 to 18 dorsal spines and 11 to 13 soft rays on the dorsal fin, while the anal fin carries three spines and nine to eleven soft rays; the vertebral count ranges from 30 to 32. The head is proportionally small, and even mature males have only modestly enlarged jaws, the lower jaw measuring about 29–37 % of the head length. Male breeding individuals lack the tasselled genital papilla found in some other species. The body depth reaches roughly 36–50 % of the fish’s standard length. A striking feature at every life stage is the presence of regular vertical stripes that run through the entire depth of the caudal (tail) fin; in smaller individuals these stripes are broader, form an arc, and begin at the fin’s base. Adult males are generally bluish‑pink, sometimes showing a darker throat, belly, anal, and pelvic fins, whereas females are usually brownish on top with a silvery‑white underside and exhibit about ten thin vertical bars.

Nemipterus celebicus.description: The fish has a total of ten dorsal spines and nine soft rays, along with three anal spines and seven anal soft rays. It lacks a suborbital spine, and the preopercle bears three transverse rows of scales. Its pectoral fins are long, extending to a point between the anus and the origin of the anal fin, while the pelvic fins are very elongated, reaching the level of—or even extending beyond—the start of the anal fin. The upper lobe of the caudal (tail) fin is slightly rounded and has a rosy hue. A distinct line runs upward from the rear edge of the suborbital area to the dorsal profile, meeting it about two to four scales before the dorsal fin begins, and an axillary scale is present. The fish’s coloration is pinkish on the upper body, fading to silvery‑white on the underside, with two silvery‑mauve lines positioned in front of and below the eye. Its body shape is fusiform and normal, with an oval cross‑section.

Rastrelliger Faughni.description: The fish has a streamlined, fusiform body with an oval cross‑section and a head that is longer than the depth of its body. It possesses eight to eleven dorsal spines and twelve soft dorsal rays, while the anal fin lacks spines and contains twelve soft rays, with the anal spine being only rudimentary. A total of thirty‑one vertebrae support its shape, and a small, single interpelvic process is present. Its maxilla is covered by the lachrymal bone, and a functional swim bladder helps it maintain buoyancy. The gill rakers are relatively short, extending only a little into the mouth, and the longest ones are bristly, numbering between thirty and fifty‑five on each side. A distinctive black blotch sits just behind the base of the pectoral fin, and the belly displays a yellow‑silver hue. Between two and six large spots are often seen at the base of the first dorsal fin, and some individuals show two faint stripes running along the level of the lateral line.

Saurida Undosquamis.description: The fish has no dorsal spines and twelve soft rays on its dorsal fin, and its anal fin also lacks spines and has about twelve soft rays. Its body is cigar‑shaped—long and slightly rounded or compressed—with a pointed, flattened head and a rounded snout. The dorsal fin begins nearer the small adipose fin than to the tip of the snout, while the anal fin starts closer to the base of the tail than to the gill cover. Its coloration is a brown‑gray shade on the top that fades to a creamy hue underneath, and the sides display eight to ten faint, darker spots running down the middle. Overall, the fish has an elongated, circular cross‑section shape.
